KEY MESSAGE 1: A strong low pressure system will track northward from interior North Carolina into western Pennsylvania this afternoon. The overall track of the low has not changed in recent model runs with the only difference being a 2-3 hour delay in the onset of precipitation across our forecast area. The track is favorable for strong warm air advection in the low and mid-levels which will be supportive of widespread rainfall across the region tonight into Friday morning. Given the initial cold currently overhead, we expect this warm air to overrun the cold air at the summits and some valley locations leading to a period of freezing rain this evening and overnight tonight. Freezing rain totals generally have stayed the same across the high terrain and sheltered valleys but we have increased icing totals across the St. Lawrence Valley significantly. Earlier in the day, there was some question about how cold the northeasterly winds would be throughout the valley with the high pressure system to the north. It's becoming increasingly clear that the St. Lawrence Valley will be able to advect in air in the 28-31 degree range through much of the event, leading to freezing rain accumulation up to a quarter of an inch. With this load of icing and winds gusting up to 30 mph, it's possible that we see a few localized power outages due to the weight of the ice and increased stress from the winds. Eventually, sometime Friday morning, temperatures will warm above freezing with all precipitation changing to rain. Once a cold front comes through later in the day on Friday, we will see a mix of mountain snow showers and valley rain showers continue off and on in the northwesterly flow through Saturday. KEY MESSAGE 2: Models continue to show a strong low level jet moving overhead this evening with 900 mb winds approaching 60 knots. This will lead to strong winds mid-mountain and summit level with some gap winds impacting Rutland County. Right now, it seems like 35-45 mph winds will be possible in Rutland County tonight with 45 to 60 mph possible as you get closer to summit level. Elsewhere, winds don't appear to be nearly as strong with max wind gusts in the 15 to 25 mph range. As noted earlier, the channeled northeasterly winds in the St. Lawrence Valley could top 30 mph which when combined with icing could create some utility outages. Across southern Vermont, we expect isolated outages as a result of the stronger winds but outages will likely be limited to Rutland and Bennington Counties. If precipitation lingers, it could stabilize the boundary layer and reduce mixing and therefor the maximum wind gusts. WCAX METEOROLOGIST (regional station — Burlington relevance only, never their branding): BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) -Happy Thanksgiving! The bulk of the Thanksgiving holiday is looking quiet and dry. We will notice more cloud cover through the day, but we look to stay dry through at least Thanksgiving evening and night. Rain showers and some high terrain mountain snow showers arrive to the south on Thanksgiving evening and push northward through the night. Overnight lows are in the mid to upper 30s for most. There could be some icing at the very onset of this system to start, with a few communities in higher terrain spots maybe running a glaze of icing. I am not expecting any big issues on the main roads, but a few secondary roads could become a tad slick tonight, especially in higher terrain spots. Black Friday will see any mountain mixed precipitation transition into mainly rain, and rain could be heavier at times, especially through the morning hours and becoming a bit more scattered by Friday evening and night. The other big component to this system looks to be the wind. That is why we have gone ahead and issued a First Alert Weather Day for Friday. The real bullseye for the wind will be right along the western slopes of the mountains, where they could see gusts upwards of 40-60 MPH. This could be enough to result in scattered power outages Friday. Intensity will vary widely over short distances. Ridgelines and communities on or near the western mountain slopes again could see a window of gusts as high as 40 to 60 mph early Friday. Conditions have to come together in the right way to see the higher end gusts make it to the ground. We usually see wind gusts intensify when rain slows down or stops. Gusts will be much less intense away from the western slopes. Some areas won’t see much wind at all. The strongest gusts will likely occur early Friday morning before sunrise, especially if there is a lull in precipitation. Wind will trend lighter through the morning and into Friday afternoon. Saturday looks drier overall, but there could still be a few scattered showers and mountain snow showers from time to time. Temperatures are again in the low to mid 40s. Winds look to be calmer through the day Saturday. By Sunday, most of us are back to dry conditions, but cloudy as temperatures continue to warm by a few degrees and we head back towards the mid and upper 40s and lower 50s. Into next week a few showers are possible by Monday with temperatures again in the mid to upper 40s.
NBC5 METEOROLOGIST (2026-11-25T23:35:00Z — same caveat): Rain, ice, wind late on Thanksgiving — Thanksgiving starts dry, with some sun, before clouds thicken up by afternoon. A coastal low sends in steady rain by evening and overnight, which may start as an icy mix in the mountains. Highs reach the low 40s. Strong downslope wind will cause issues Thursday night into Friday morning. Bennington County is where the most outages will be, with 70 mph gust potential. Some will also occur in eastern Rutland and Addison counties. By daytime Friday, less wind. Expect a cloudy sky with scattered rain showers through the morning and a steadier round of rain in by late afternoon. A few snowflakes may mix in for the mountains, especially late. This weekend brings lingering showers of rain and mountain snow (especially Saturday), lots of clouds and a mild feel. Highs reach the 40s to around 50. More sun by Sunday.
